props.title: Salesman
props.initialSlug: Four door-to-door Bible salesmen chase the American dream

sections.content: Salesman revolutionized documentary filmmaking through its raw, intimate portrayal of four door-to-door Bible salesmen. The Maysles brothers and Charlotte Zwerin captured the crushing reality of the American Dream's dark side, predating similar themes in Glengarry Glen Ross (1992) and Death of a Salesman (1985). Their innovative "direct cinema" approach, using handheld cameras and natural lighting, influenced countless documentarians including Barbara Kopple's Harlan County USA (1976) and Steve James' Hoop Dreams (1994).

sections.content: The film's main subject, Paul "The Badger" Brennan, becomes an unforgettable portrait of quiet desperation. His declining sales and growing disillusionment mirror themes later explored in fictional works like The Big Short (2015) and Inside Job (2010). The Maysles' observational style catches every micro-expression, every defeated slump of shoulders, creating an unprecedented level of psychological intimacy that influenced later character studies like American Movie (1999).

The film's exploration of religious commercialization remains startlingly relevant, connecting to later documentaries like Jesus Camp (2006) and Marjoe (1972). The salesmen's practiced pitches and manipulation techniques expose the intersection of faith and capitalism, themes that would later emerge in works like There Will Be Blood (2007) and Elmer Gantry (1960). sections.content: Salesman's influence extends into modern documentary techniques, visible in works like The Queen of Versailles (2012) and Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010). Its unflinching examination of failure and desperation created a template for character-driven documentaries that prioritize observation over intervention. The film's ability to extract universal truths from specific experiences influenced later works like Man on Wire (2008) and Amy (2015).
